transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-09-10 14:00 PDT | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Priya Ramesh (Quantaco Head of ML), Ethan Park (SRE), Sara Kim (Product)

Summary (auto-gen, sometimes noisy): Quick weekly sync to review cost/unit economics from last week's benchmark, discuss caching and batching tradeoffs, and agree next steps for a longer 24h production-shaped run.

00:00 Maya: okay hi everyone, thanks for joining, we're on for 45 minutes, main agenda is cost per token, tokens per second per dollar, and caching savings from prefix caching we configured last week.
00:18 Priya: hey thanks, yes we've been looking at the spreadsheet you sent, a few numbers look off on our end i think -- maybe the tokenization difference?
00:30 Luis: yeah there can be tokenization deltas, we used GPT-style tokenizer for the estimates, quantaco's tokenization for your model variant is about 5-8% higher which explains some of the variance.
00:45 Ethan: that makes sense, one quick ask, when you say tokens/sec/$ can you remind us the baseline assumptions? i.e. instance type, quantization, batch size?
01:05 Maya: absolutely, baseline for the slide was A100-40GB equivalent throughput with 8-bit quantized model, batching window 50ms, concurrency 16, and we assumed prefix cache hit rate 20% for conversational workloads. that produced roughly 2,900 tokens/sec per dollar in our estimate.
01:35 Priya: 2,900 tokens per second per dollar sounds high vs our internal run which showed ~1,800 at similar conditions, we should reconcile.
01:50 Luis: two quick points -- first your internal run used full attention and 16k context which increases memory movement and reduces throughput; second your tokenization delta plus shorter sequences will reduce amortized throughput.
02:10 Sara: can you spell out the cache savings again? if prefix cache hit rate goes from 20 to 50% what's the delta on cost?
02:25 Maya: rough math: with 20% cache hit we estimated 2,900 tokens/sec/$; at 50% cache hit that moves to ~4,200 tokens/sec/$ so roughly a 45% effective cost reduction on token-generation compute. that's because prefix cache avoids re-computing the KV for the prefix, so token cost becomes only the continuation tokens for many sessions.
03:02 Priya: okay that aligns with our intuition. are those numbers for hosted or dedicated?
03:10 Maya: those figures are for Redwood Dedicated equivalent pricing profile; hosted will have slightly higher unit price but same relative improvement from cache. in hosted you'd see a similar percent delta but baseline tokens/sec/$ lower by ~10-15% due to multi-tenant overhead.
03:35 Ethan: we saw some CPU bottlenecking in our sidecar for batching, our throughput didn't scale linearly with batch size, any recommendations?
03:50 Luis: yeah sidecar CPU and network can become the limiter. we recommend moving batching into runtime (continuous batching) instead of client-side micro-batches; also tune batching window - for your workload 30-60ms window with concurrency 8-12 gave best p95. larger windows improved throughput but increased tail latency.
04:20 Priya: so there's a latency tradeoff -- if we increase batch window for better tokens/$ we might violate our p99 SLA, what's typical tradeoff curve?
04:35 Luis: typical tradeoff: going from 30ms to 100ms batching window can improve tokens/sec/$ by ~25-40% depending on sequence length distribution, but p99 latency can degrade by 40-100ms. if p99 SLO is strict we'd target smaller windows and rely on caching to get cost benefits.
05:05 Sara: what about quantization tradeoffs? we care about quality regression - 8-bit vs 4-bit?
05:15 Maya: 8-bit quant usually maintains near-parity on most evals; 4-bit can save more but sometimes needs per-layer calibration and can introduce regressions on some prompts. for production we'd recommend 8-bit initially, run focused evals on your prompt-set, then consider selective 4-bit for non-critical routes.
05:45 Ethan: can we get config examples to try? our infra team prefers immutable configs so a one-page snippet would help.
05:55 Luis: yes i'll share the batching config, prefix cache TTL example, and recommended concurrency/threads. will include notes about sidecar CPU limits.
06:10 Priya: one odd thing in your cost sheet - the amortization of model load across sessions, how do you handle cold-starts?
06:25 Maya: our cost model includes a small per-session amortized cost assuming pool reuse; cold-starts were charged separately in the benchmark but we also show an amortized view where the first N requests pay the model load over an hour. we can add a separate sheet that shows pure steady-state vs cold-start ops.
07:00 Priya: good, please add that.
07:10 Ethan: question about encryption and KMS overhead - does enabling customer KMS materially change throughput/cost?
07:25 Maya: negligible on inference throughput because encryption is for storage of keys and request metadata; there can be small latency added on key fetches if not cached, but normally that's in the 5-10ms range and we recommend caching keys in HSM client. we'll document best practices.
07:55 Sara: back to numbers, can you run a 24h bench with realistic traffic? last week the short run had spike variance.
08:05 Maya: yes that's one of the next steps, Ethan to run 24h with prod-shaped traffic; Redwood will provide the runner and config to ensure comparability.
08:18 Priya: also include a run with prefix-cache off so we can see absolute delta.
08:25 Luis: good idea, we'll do paired runs: cache on/off, batching window small/medium, quant 8-bit vs 4-bit. that should give a matrix of measurements.
08:45 Ethan: for matrix size, how many permutations are we talking? we have limited infra budget...
08:55 Luis: start with the 4 main combos: (cache on/off) x (batching 30ms/100ms) x (8-bit/4-bit) but that's 8 runs; you can prioritize 4 runs and we'll extrapolate.
09:20 Priya: what's the expected cost delta between 8-bit and 4-bit on tokens/sec/$?
09:30 Maya: 4-bit can boost tokens/sec/$ by ~20-50% depending on kernel availability and sequence length, but quality risk must be measured. 8-bit is safest for initial production.
09:50 Sara: any other constraints we should be aware of before trying 4-bit? e.g., model architecture, custom ops?
10:00 Luis: yes some models need kernel support, and some transformer variants behave poorly with aggressive quant. we'll flag per-model compatibility in the summary doc.
10:20 Priya: okay sounds good. next step for us is to confirm the SLA targets and run the 24h bench.
10:30 Maya: perfect. I'll send the updated cost workbook and the Redwood recommended configs; Luis will include the one-pager; Ethan will run bench and we reconvene after results.

Transcript notes: some transcription artifacts present (speaker overlaps, minor mis-words like "prefix cash" instead of "prefix cache"), speakers labeled by name but sometimes cut.

Recap (manual):
- Primary focus: reconcile token/sec/$ figures between Redwood estimates and Quantaco's internal runs. biggest levers: cache hit rate, batching window, quantization level, tokenization differences.
- Redwood estimate: ~2,900 tokens/sec/$ baseline (dedicated, 8-bit, 20% cache hit, 50ms window). Quantaco observed ~1,800 in their short run (16k context, different tokenizer).
- Cache impact: moving to 50% hit could raise tokens/sec/$ to ~4,200 (approx +45%).
- Batching: larger windows improve tokens/$ but increase tail latency; tradeoff analysis needed vs p99 SLO.
- Quantization: 8-bit recommended initially; 4-bit possible with selective evaluation due to quality risk.

End of transcript.
